sectionTitle: Forces and motion: Forces, accelerations and Newton's Laws of motion

specStatements.text: Newton’s First Law:
If the resultant force acting on an object is zero and:
• the object is stationary, the object remains stationary
• the object is moving, the object continues to move at the same speed and in the same direction. So the object continues to move at the same velocity.
So, when a vehicle travels at a steady speed the resistive forces balance the driving force.
So, the velocity (speed and/or direction) of an object will only change if a resultant force is acting on the object.
Students should be able to apply Newton’s First Law to explain the motion of objects moving with a uniform velocity and objects where the speed and/or direction changes.
(HT only) The tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion is called inertia.
Newton’s Second Law:
The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on the object, and inversely proportional to the mass of the object.
As an equation:
resultant force = mass × acceleration
F = m a
force, F, in newtons, N
mass, m, in kilograms, kg
acceleration, a, in metres per second squared, m/s^2
(HT only) Students should be able to explain that:
• inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object
• inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration.
Students should be able to estimate the speed, accelerations and forces involved in large accelerations for everyday road transport.
Students should recognise and be able to use the symbol that indicates an approximate value or approximate answer, ̴

Required practical activity 7: investigate the effect of varying the force on the acceleration of an object of constant mass, and the effect of varying the mass of an object on the acceleration produced by a constant force.
AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1, 2 and 3.
This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
Newton’s Third Law:
Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite.
Students should be able to apply Newton’s Third Law to examples of equilibrium situations.

scopeNotes.statement: AT skills covered by this practical activity: AT 1, 2 and 3.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The apparatus-and-techniques statements are treated as a boundary on what required practical activity 7 may be asked about, not as content to be recalled. Questions on the practical stay inside AT 1 (use of apparatus to make and record measurements accurately - the trolley's mass, the hanging masses, the light gate separation and the times), AT 2 (use of apparatus to observe and measure the effect of a force on the motion of an object) and AT 3 (use of apparatus and techniques to determine speed and rate of change of speed). No technique from outside those three is introduced, and the numbered AT descriptors themselves are never set as recall.

scopeNotes.statement: This practical activity also provides opportunities to develop WS and MS. Details of all skills are given in Key opportunities for skills development.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Working scientifically and mathematical skills are developed through the practical itself - identifying the independent, dependent and control variables, recognising that the total accelerating mass must be held constant, plotting acceleration against resultant force and against mass, and reading a gradient - rather than being taught or examined as a separate body of knowledge. Because this statement points to skills documented elsewhere in the specification, it carries no questions of its own and nothing here is assessed that the practical does not naturally require.

concepts.definition: If the resultant force acting on an object is zero, the object's motion does not change: a stationary object remains stationary and a moving object continues to move at the same speed and in the same direction, so at the same velocity. The law is about the resultant of the forces being zero, not about there being no forces at all.

The single force that would have the same effect as all the forces acting on an object together. When the forces balance, that resultant is zero: a stationary object then remains stationary, even though individual forces such as weight and a surface's upward push are still acting on it.

Motion at the same speed in the same direction. If the resultant force on a moving object is zero, the object continues to move at the same speed and in the same direction, so it continues to move at the same velocity. No forward force is needed to maintain that motion.

When a vehicle travels at a steady speed the resistive forces balance the driving force. The driving force from the engine and the resistive forces of friction and air resistance are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant force is zero and the velocity does not change.

The velocity (speed and/or direction) of an object will only change if a resultant force is acting on the object. A car rounding a bend at a constant speed has a changing direction, so its velocity is changing and a resultant force must be acting, even though the speedometer reading is fixed.

The tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion is called inertia. It is a tendency, not a force: passengers thrown forwards when a bus brakes are not pushed forwards, they simply keep moving at the velocity they already had while the bus slows beneath them.

The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on the object, and inversely proportional to the mass of the object. Doubling the resultant force on a fixed mass doubles the acceleration; doubling the mass under a fixed resultant force halves the acceleration.

Newton's Second Law written as an equation: resultant force = mass x acceleration, F = m a. The F in the equation is the resultant of all the forces on the object, not any single force acting on it, and the equation can be rearranged to find the mass or the acceleration.

In the equation F = m a the force, F, is in newtons, N; the mass, m, is in kilograms, kg; and the acceleration, a, is in metres per second squared, m/s^2. A mass given in grams must be converted to kilograms before it is substituted into the equation.

Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object. A large inertial mass needs a large resultant force to produce a given change of velocity, which is why a loaded lorry is far harder to speed up or slow down than a bicycle.

Inertial mass is defined as the ratio of force over acceleration. Dividing the resultant force acting on an object by the acceleration that force produces gives the object's inertial mass in kilograms, which is the same rearrangement as m = F / a taken from F = m a.

Typical everyday values let speeds, accelerations and forces be estimated for road transport: a car reaching about 27 m/s in about 9 s accelerates at roughly 3 m/s^2, and with a mass of about 1000 kg that needs a resultant force of roughly 3000 N. Large accelerations demand correspondingly large forces.

The symbol ~ placed before a value indicates an approximate value or an approximate answer. Writing 'resultant force ~ 3000 N' says the figure is an estimate of the right order, obtained from rounded data, and not a precisely measured or exactly calculated result.

concepts.term: Required practical activity 7: force and acceleration
concepts.definition: An investigation of the effect of varying the force on the acceleration of an object of constant mass. A trolley is pulled by hanging masses on a string over a pulley and the acceleration is found from light gate timings. The total mass being accelerated must be kept constant, so masses are moved from the trolley to the hanger to change the force.

concepts.term: Required practical activity 7: mass and acceleration
concepts.definition: The second part of the same practical investigates the effect of varying the mass of an object on the acceleration produced by a constant force. With the pulling force fixed, extra masses are added to the trolley and the acceleration is measured each time; the acceleration falls as the mass rises, because acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.

Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite. If a swimmer pushes back on the water with 200 N, the water pushes the swimmer forwards with 200 N. The two forces are always the same size, whatever the sizes of the two objects.

In an equilibrium situation such as a book resting on a table, the third law pair is the book's downward push on the table and the table's upward push on the book. These act on different objects, so they never cancel; the book's weight and the table's upward push act on the same object and are balanced forces, not a third law pair.

misconceptions.question: A puck slides across smooth ice at a steady speed. Is a forward force acting on it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Its velocity is not changing, so the resultant force on it is zero.
misconceptions.misconception: Something must be pushing it forwards, or it would stop; a moving object needs a force to keep it moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everything that moves in ordinary life does stop, because friction and air resistance act on it. Students generalise from that and treat motion, rather than change of motion, as the thing needing a cause.
misconceptions.correction: A resultant force changes velocity; it does not maintain it. Remove friction and air resistance and the puck keeps its velocity indefinitely with no forward force at all.

misconceptions.question: A crate sits still on a floor. What forces act on it?
misconceptions.correct: Its weight acts down and the floor's push acts up; these are equal, so the resultant is zero.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing is happening to the crate, so no forces act on it at all.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read 'the resultant force is zero' as 'there is no force', because the two phrases describe the same visible outcome - an object that does not move.
misconceptions.correction: Zero resultant is not the same as no forces. Several forces can act and still add to nothing; remove the floor and the weight alone would show itself at once.

misconceptions.question: An object moves at a constant velocity. Which way does the resultant force point?
misconceptions.correct: There is no resultant force, since the velocity is constant.
misconceptions.misconception: There must be a small backwards resultant force, because everything gradually slows down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Real objects are slowed by friction and drag, so students carry that experience into questions that explicitly say those forces can be ignored.
misconceptions.correction: Read the question: if resistive forces are negligible or balanced, the resultant is zero and the speed does not fall at all.

misconceptions.question: A van travels along a level road at a steady 25 m/s. How do the forces compare?
misconceptions.correct: The resistive forces balance the driving force, so the resultant force is zero.
misconceptions.misconception: The driving force must be bigger than the resistive forces, otherwise the van would not keep going.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate a large driving force with fast motion rather than with acceleration, and think that staying in motion requires a surplus of force.
misconceptions.correction: A surplus of driving force would make the van speed up. A steady speed is the signature of balanced forces and a zero resultant.

misconceptions.question: A car drives round a roundabout at a constant 10 m/s. Is there a resultant force on it?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The direction is changing, so the velocity is changing and a resultant force must act.
misconceptions.misconception: No, because the speed on the speedometer never changes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Speed and velocity are used interchangeably in everyday speech, so a fixed speedometer reading is taken to mean nothing about the motion is changing.
misconceptions.correction: Velocity includes direction. A change of direction alone is a change of velocity, and that requires a resultant force.

misconceptions.question: What is inertia?
misconceptions.correct: The tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion.
misconceptions.misconception: Inertia is a forward force that a moving object carries with it and gradually uses up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word is used loosely outside physics, and describing motion as 'having momentum' or 'carrying force' makes inertia sound like a stored push.
misconceptions.correction: Inertia is a tendency, not a force. It appears in free body diagrams nowhere at all; what it describes is the absence of any need for a force to keep velocity constant.

misconceptions.question: Two trolleys travel at the same speed, one heavy and one light. Which has more inertia?
misconceptions.correct: The heavier one, because inertia depends on mass, not on how fast the object is going.
misconceptions.misconception: The faster an object is travelling, the more inertia it has.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fast objects are visibly harder to stop, so students tie the tendency to keep moving to the speed rather than to the mass.
misconceptions.correction: Inertia is the tendency to keep the state of motion, and it is measured by inertial mass. A stationary lorry has an enormous inertia while at rest.

misconceptions.question: The resultant force on a trolley of fixed mass is doubled. What happens?
misconceptions.correct: The acceleration doubles, because acceleration is proportional to the resultant force.
misconceptions.misconception: The speed doubles, because twice the force makes it go twice as fast.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language links force to speed - pressing harder on the pedal 'makes it go faster' - and speed is easier to picture than rate of change of speed.
misconceptions.correction: Force sets the acceleration, not the speed. Twice the force means the velocity climbs twice as quickly, and the final speed depends on how long the force acts.

misconceptions.question: The same resultant force acts on a trolley whose mass has been trebled. What happens to the acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: It falls to a third, because acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.
misconceptions.misconception: It trebles, because a bigger mass means a bigger acceleration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect the two quantities in a law to rise together, and heavy falling objects seem to 'go harder', so proportionality is applied where inverse proportionality is meant.
misconceptions.correction: In a = F / m the mass is on the bottom. Treble the mass under the same resultant force and the acceleration drops to one third.

misconceptions.question: A car's engine provides 3000 N while drag and friction total 1000 N. The car's mass is 1000 kg. What is its acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: 2 m/s^2, using the resultant force of 2000 N in F = m a.
misconceptions.misconception: 3 m/s^2, using the 3000 N driving force in the equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is remembered as 'force = mass x acceleration' without the word resultant, so the most prominent force in the question is substituted straight in.
misconceptions.correction: The F in F = m a is always the resultant. Combine all the forces first, then divide by the mass.

misconceptions.question: A 400 g trolley has a resultant force of 0.8 N on it. What is its acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: 2 m/s^2, after converting the mass to 0.4 kg.
misconceptions.misconception: 0.002 m/s^2, using the mass as 400 in the equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number is given in grams and substituted without conversion, because the unit looks like a mass unit and the equation does not say which one to use.
misconceptions.correction: In F = m a the mass, m, is in kilograms, kg. Convert grams to kilograms before substituting, dividing by 1000.

misconceptions.question: What are the units of acceleration in F = m a?
misconceptions.correct: Metres per second squared, m/s^2.
misconceptions.misconception: Metres per second, m/s, because acceleration is about how fast something goes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Acceleration is described in words as a speed changing, and the squared second has no everyday meaning to attach it to.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration is a change of velocity in m/s divided by a time in s, so its unit carries a second twice over: m/s^2.

misconceptions.question: What does the inertial mass of an object measure?
misconceptions.correct: How difficult it is to change the velocity of the object.
misconceptions.misconception: It measures the pull of gravity on the object, in newtons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass and weight are used as synonyms outside physics, and bathroom scales report a gravitational effect as though it were a mass.
misconceptions.correction: Inertial mass is about resisting a change of velocity, and it is measured in kilograms. It would be unchanged on the Moon, where the gravitational pull is not.

misconceptions.question: How is inertial mass defined?
misconceptions.correct: As the ratio of force over acceleration.
misconceptions.misconception: You get the answer by carrying out the operation the wrong way round — multiplying two quantities where you should divide one by the other, or dividing them the wrong way up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Ratio' is remembered without its order, and either arrangement of the two quantities looks equally plausible on the page.
misconceptions.correction: Force over acceleration, matching m = F / a from F = m a. Check with units: N divided by m/s^2 gives kg.

misconceptions.question: Estimate the acceleration of a car that reaches about 27 m/s from rest in about 9 s.
misconceptions.correct: About 3 m/s^2, from a velocity change of 27 m/s over 9 s.
misconceptions.misconception: About 27 m/s^2, because that is how fast the car is going.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In an estimation question the most prominent number is quoted back with the units of whatever is asked for, without the division being done.
misconceptions.correction: An estimate still needs the calculation. Divide the change of velocity by the time before rounding to a sensible one figure value.

misconceptions.question: A student writes 'resultant force ~ 3000 N'. What does the symbol mean?
misconceptions.correct: That 3000 N is an approximate value, not an exact one.
misconceptions.misconception: That the force is smaller than 3000 N.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The symbol is confused with the inequality signs learned in mathematics, which do set an upper or a lower limit on a value.
misconceptions.correction: The symbol indicates an approximate value or approximate answer. The true value may lie either side of the figure quoted.

misconceptions.question: In required practical 7, how is the force on the trolley varied without changing the accelerating mass?
misconceptions.correct: By moving masses from the trolley to the hanger, so the total mass stays the same.
misconceptions.misconception: By adding extra masses to the hanger, leaving the trolley loaded as it was.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The hanging masses are seen as the source of the force and the trolley as the object, so students forget that the hanging masses are accelerating too.
misconceptions.correction: The string accelerates the trolley and the hanging masses together. Transfer masses rather than adding them, so the total accelerating mass is constant.

misconceptions.question: In the second part of the practical the force is constant and mass is added to the trolley. What is seen?
misconceptions.correct: The acceleration falls, because it is inversely proportional to the mass.
misconceptions.misconception: The acceleration stays the same, because the pulling force has not been changed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students latch onto the constant quantity named in the question and assume that whatever depends on it must also stay constant.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration depends on both quantities. With F fixed, a = F / m falls as m rises, giving a curve rather than a horizontal line.

misconceptions.question: A swimmer pushes back on the water with 200 N. What force does the water exert on the swimmer?
misconceptions.correct: 200 N forwards, since the forces two objects exert on each other are equal and opposite.
misconceptions.misconception: Less than 200 N, because the water is pushed aside so easily.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students expect the sturdier or heavier object to win the exchange, and read 'equal and opposite' as applying only to evenly matched objects.
misconceptions.correction: The pair is always equal in size, whatever the two objects are. A fly striking a lorry pushes on it exactly as hard as the lorry pushes back.

misconceptions.question: If the forces two objects exert on each other are equal and opposite, how can anything accelerate?
misconceptions.correct: The two forces act on different objects, so they never cancel on either one.
misconceptions.misconception: They do cancel, so a horse can never actually get a cart moving.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balanced forces and third law pairs both come as 'equal and opposite', and students add the two forces together as though they acted on one body.
misconceptions.correction: Only forces on the same object can be added. The cart accelerates because of the forces on the cart alone; the cart's pull acts on the horse.

misconceptions.question: A book rests on a table. Which two forces form a Newton's Third Law pair?
misconceptions.correct: The book's downward push on the table and the table's upward push on the book.
misconceptions.misconception: The book's weight and the table's upward push on the book.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Those two forces are equal and opposite in this situation, which is exactly the phrase used for a third law pair, so the label is attached to the wrong pair.
misconceptions.correction: A third law pair acts on two different objects and is the same kind of force. Weight and the table's push both act on the book, so they are balanced forces.

misconceptions.question: A puck slides at 4 m/s with friction negligible. What is the resultant force on it?
misconceptions.correct: Zero, because the velocity of the puck is not changing.
misconceptions.misconception: A number given or just worked out can be written down as the answer even if it is a different quantity, such as a speed used as a force or a force used as an acceleration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: When no calculation seems possible, the only number in the question is reused with whatever unit the answer requires.
misconceptions.correction: A speed in m/s cannot become a force in N. Decide first whether the velocity is changing; if it is not, the resultant force is zero.

misconceptions.question: A book rests on a table. How does the table's upward push compare with the book's weight?
misconceptions.correct: They are equal in size, so the resultant force on the book is zero.
misconceptions.misconception: The table must push up harder than the weight pulls down, or the book would not be held up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Holding something up feels like an effort, so students assume that supporting an object needs a surplus of upward force.
misconceptions.correction: A surplus upward force would accelerate the book upwards off the table. Holding it still needs the two forces to be equal, giving a zero resultant.

misconceptions.question: The resultant force on a trolley is doubled and its mass is unchanged. What happens to the acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: It doubles, because acceleration is proportional to the resultant force.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing changes, because the mass of the trolley is the same as it was.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Half of the second law is remembered - that acceleration depends on mass - so a question that leaves the mass alone looks like a question with no change in it.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration depends on both quantities: proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to the mass. Change either one and the acceleration changes.

misconceptions.question: A car of mass 1200 kg accelerates at 2.5 m/s^2. What resultant force acts on it?
misconceptions.correct: 3000 N, from mass x acceleration.
misconceptions.misconception: 480 N or 1202.5 N, from dividing or adding the two numbers given.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is recalled as a link between three quantities without its operation, so any arithmetic that uses both numbers looks defensible.
misconceptions.correction: resultant force = mass x acceleration is a multiplication. Check the answer with units: kg x m/s^2 gives N.

misconceptions.question: In required practical 7, which quantity is the dependent variable?
misconceptions.correct: The acceleration of the trolley, which is measured for each force used.
misconceptions.misconception: The acceleration must be kept constant, because it is the quantity the experiment is about.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Control variables and the measured outcome are both described as things you 'look after' in a practical, so students hold the outcome fixed as well.
misconceptions.correction: The acceleration is what you measure and it must be free to change. Only the total accelerating mass is controlled in the first part of the practical.

misconceptions.question: A swimmer pushes backwards on the water. Which way does the water's force on her act?
misconceptions.correct: Forwards, opposite to the direction of her push on the water.
misconceptions.misconception: Backwards, in the same direction as the force she applies.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students match the size of the pair correctly but keep the direction of the original push, because the word 'equal' is remembered more firmly than the word 'opposite'.
misconceptions.correction: The forces two interacting objects exert on each other are equal AND opposite. If they acted the same way, no swimmer could ever move forwards.

misconceptions.question: Can two forces that both act on the same object be a Newton's Third Law pair?
misconceptions.correct: No. A third law pair is one force on each of the two interacting objects.
misconceptions.misconception: Yes, as long as the two forces are equal in size they are a pair.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The test students remember is 'equal and opposite', which several pairs of forces in a diagram satisfy, so the object each force acts on is never checked.
misconceptions.correction: Identify the two objects first. One force of the pair acts on each of them; two forces drawn on one object can never be a third law pair.

mcqs.stem: A crate rests on a level floor. Its weight is 400 N downwards and the floor pushes upwards on it with a force of 400 N. Which statement about the crate is correct?

options.text: The resultant force on the crate is zero, so it stays stationary.
options.rationale: The two forces are equal in size and opposite in direction, so the resultant force is zero, and a stationary object with zero resultant force remains stationary.

options.text: No force at all acts on the crate while it is not moving.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read 'nothing is happening' as 'no forces', although the question names two of them.

options.text: The crate's weight and the floor's push are a third law pair.
options.rationale: The forces are equal and opposite, so the third law label is attached to them; both act on the crate, so they are balanced forces.

options.text: The two forces add up to 800 N pressing on the floor.
options.rationale: Picked by students who add force sizes and ignore that the two forces point in opposite directions.

mcqs.stem: A puck slides in a straight line across a level ice rink at a steady 4 m/s. Friction and air resistance are so small that they can be ignored. What is the resultant force on the puck?

options.text: It acts forwards, because the puck is still moving forwards.
options.rationale: The commonest error in mechanics: treating motion itself, rather than change of motion, as the thing that needs a force.

options.text: It is zero, because the puck's velocity is not changing.
options.rationale: The speed and the direction are both constant, so the velocity is constant, and by Newton's First Law the resultant force must be zero.

options.text: It acts backwards, so the puck is very slowly stopping.
options.rationale: Students who expect every moving object to slow down override the statement that friction can be ignored.

options.text: It is 4 N forwards, matching the puck's steady speed.
options.rationale: Reuses the only number in the question as a force, a substitution made when no calculation seems available.

mcqs.stem: A van travels along a straight level road at a steady 25 m/s. The driving force from its engine is 900 N. What can be said about the resistive forces on the van?

options.text: They are smaller than 900 N, which is why the van moves.
options.rationale: Students think staying in motion needs a surplus of driving force, when a surplus would make the van speed up.

options.text: They are larger than 900 N, so the van is losing speed.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume drag always wins in the end, ignoring the stated steady speed.

options.text: They total 900 N, acting backwards along the road.
options.rationale: At a steady speed the resistive forces balance the driving force, so together they come to 900 N in the opposite direction.

options.text: They are zero, as the road surface is smooth.
options.rationale: Confuses a level road with a frictionless one; air resistance alone rules this out at 25 m/s.

mcqs.stem: A car is driven all the way round a roundabout at a constant speed of 10 m/s. Is there a resultant force acting on the car?

options.text: No, since the speed stays at a steady 10 m/s.
options.rationale: Treats a fixed speedometer reading as proof that nothing about the motion is changing.

options.text: No, the forces on the car must all be balanced.
options.rationale: Follows from reading constant speed as constant velocity, so the resultant is assumed to be zero.

options.text: Only if the driver presses the brake pedal.
options.rationale: Assumes a resultant force is present only while the speed is being changed deliberately.

options.text: Yes, because its direction is changing.
options.rationale: Velocity is speed and direction. The direction changes continuously, so the velocity changes, and velocity only changes if a resultant force acts.

mcqs.stem: A skydiver falls at a constant terminal velocity before opening her parachute. Which statement explains her motion?

options.text: Her weight has fallen to zero, so nothing is pulling her downwards.
options.rationale: Students who know the resultant is zero conclude that the weight itself must have gone.

options.text: Her weight and the air resistance are equal, so the resultant is zero.
options.rationale: A constant velocity means a zero resultant force, which here means the upward air resistance has grown until it balances her downward weight exactly.

options.text: The air resistance is now larger than her weight as she falls.
options.rationale: A surplus upward force is assumed, which would in fact slow her down rather than hold the speed steady.

options.text: A downward resultant force keeps her moving downwards at speed.
options.rationale: Treats continued motion as needing a force in the direction of travel.

mcqs.stem: A book lies at rest on a table. Which statement about the forces on the book is correct?

options.text: There are no forces on the book while it lies still.
options.rationale: Reads a zero resultant as an absence of forces, the most common confusion about the first law.

options.text: The table's push must be bigger, to hold the book up.
options.rationale: Students think holding something up requires a surplus force, which would send the book upwards.

options.text: Its weight and the table's push give a resultant of zero.
options.rationale: Two forces act on the book, downward weight and the table's upward push; they are equal and opposite, so the resultant force on the book is zero.

options.text: The book's weight is bigger, but the table is far too solid.
options.rationale: Invents a strength property of the table instead of comparing the two forces on the book.

mcqs.stem: (Higher tier) What is meant by the inertia of an object?

options.text: A forward force that keeps a moving object going.
options.rationale: Turns a tendency into a force, so inertia is imagined as a push carried along by the object.

options.text: A property that increases as an object moves faster.
options.rationale: Ties inertia to speed rather than to mass, because fast things look harder to stop.

options.text: The resistance of the air to an object moving through it.
options.rationale: Confuses inertia with drag, since both are described as opposing changes in motion.

options.text: Its tendency to stay at rest or in uniform motion.
options.rationale: Inertia is exactly the tendency of objects to continue in their state of rest or of uniform motion.

mcqs.stem: (Higher tier) A bus brakes sharply and the standing passengers lurch forwards. Why does this happen?

options.text: They keep moving at their original velocity.
options.rationale: Inertia: with no resultant backward force on them, the passengers continue in their state of uniform motion while the bus slows beneath them.

options.text: A forward force throws them out of their places.
options.rationale: Invents a forward push to explain forward motion, the classic force-for-motion error.

options.text: Their inertia acts as a forward push on their bodies.
options.rationale: Treats inertia as a force that can appear in the explanation as a push.

options.text: The braking force acts on the bus and then on them.
options.rationale: Assumes the braking force is transmitted to the passengers, which would push them backwards, not forwards.

mcqs.stem: The resultant force acting on a trolley is doubled while its mass is unchanged. What happens to the acceleration of the trolley?

options.text: Its speed doubles, but the acceleration stays as it was.
options.rationale: Links force to speed rather than to rate of change of speed, as everyday language does.

options.text: It halves, because the force has more work to do now.
options.rationale: Applies an inverse relationship to the force, which belongs to the mass instead.

options.text: It doubles, as acceleration is proportional to the resultant force.
options.rationale: Newton's Second Law: the acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force acting on the object, so twice the force gives twice the acceleration.

options.text: It is unchanged, since the trolley's mass is the same.
options.rationale: Remembers only the mass half of the second law and ignores the force half.

mcqs.stem: The mass of a trolley is trebled while the resultant force acting on it is kept the same. What happens to its acceleration?

options.text: It trebles, because the trolley is three times heavier.
options.rationale: Expects the two quantities to rise together, applying proportionality where the law is inverse.

options.text: It stays the same, since the force is unchanged.
options.rationale: Fixes on the constant quantity and assumes everything depending on it is constant too.

options.text: It falls to a ninth of the value it had before.
options.rationale: Imports an inverse square relationship from other topics into a simple inverse one.

options.text: The acceleration falls to a third of its old value.
options.rationale: Acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass of the object, so three times the mass under the same resultant force gives one third of the acceleration.

mcqs.stem: A car of mass 1200 kg has a resultant force acting on it that gives it an acceleration of 2.5 m/s^2. What is the size of that resultant force?

options.rationale: resultant force = mass x acceleration, so F = 1200 kg x 2.5 m/s^2 = 3000 N.
Adds the mass and the acceleration instead of multiplying them.
Divides the acceleration by the mass, a rearrangement error in F = m a.
Divides the mass by the acceleration, which gives a number but not a force.

mcqs.stem: A go-kart and driver of total mass 500 kg have a driving force of 2500 N acting forwards on them and resistive forces of 500 N acting backwards. What is the acceleration?

options.rationale: Substitutes the 2500 N driving force into F = m a instead of the resultant force.
The resultant force is 2500 N - 500 N = 2000 N, so a = F / m = 2000 N / 500 kg = 4 m/s^2.
Divides the mass by the force, inverting the rearrangement of F = m a.
Works out the resultant force correctly but quotes it with the units of acceleration.

mcqs.stem: In the equation resultant force = mass x acceleration, which set of units must be used?

options.text: force in newtons, N; mass in kilograms, kg; acceleration in m/s
options.rationale: Keeps the mass unit right but gives acceleration the unit of speed.

options.text: force in newtons, N; mass in grams, g; acceleration in m/s^2
options.rationale: Uses grams because laboratory masses are usually labelled in grams.

options.text: force in kilograms, mass in newtons, acceleration in m/s^2
options.rationale: Swaps the units of force and mass, the usual weight and mass confusion.

options.text: force in newtons, N; mass in kilograms, kg; acceleration in m/s^2
options.rationale: The specification gives force, F, in newtons, N; mass, m, in kilograms, kg; and acceleration, a, in metres per second squared, m/s^2.

mcqs.stem: Why is acceleration measured in metres per second squared, m/s^2?

options.text: A change of velocity in m/s is divided by a time in s.
options.rationale: Acceleration is a velocity change divided by the time it takes, so its unit is m/s divided by s, which is written m/s^2.

options.text: A distance in metres is divided by a time in seconds twice.
options.rationale: Close to the truth in form but starts from distance rather than from a change of velocity.

options.text: A velocity in m/s is multiplied by the time taken.
options.rationale: Multiplying would give metre units, not m/s^2; the operation is remembered the wrong way round.

options.text: The object covers a squared distance each second.
options.rationale: Reads the squared symbol as applying to the metres rather than to the seconds.

mcqs.stem: (Higher tier) What does the inertial mass of an object measure?

options.text: The size of the gravitational pull acting on the object.
options.rationale: Substitutes weight for mass, as everyday use of the two words does.

options.text: How difficult it is to change the object's velocity.
options.rationale: Inertial mass is a measure of how difficult it is to change the velocity of an object.

options.text: How fast the object is able to travel once it is released.
options.rationale: Ties the property to speed rather than to resistance to a change of velocity.

options.text: The force needed to keep the object still on Earth.
options.rationale: Turns a property of the object into a single force reading.

mcqs.stem: (Higher tier) How is inertial mass defined?

options.text: As the acceleration divided by the force.
options.rationale: Remembers that a ratio is involved but inverts it; the units then come out wrong.

options.text: As the weight of the object divided by 10 N/kg.
options.rationale: Describes how a gravitational mass is found rather than how inertial mass is defined.

options.text: As the ratio of force over acceleration.
options.rationale: The specification defines inertial mass as the ratio of force over acceleration, matching m = F / a from F = m a.

options.text: As the force multiplied by the acceleration.
options.rationale: Replaces division with multiplication, giving a quantity that is not a mass at all.

mcqs.stem: A family car reaches a speed of about 27 m/s from rest in about 9 s. Estimate its acceleration.

options.text: ~3 m/s^2, from a gain of about 27 m/s in about 9 s
options.rationale: Dividing the change of velocity by the time gives 27 / 9 = 3, so the acceleration is about 3 m/s^2, quoted as an approximate value.

options.text: ~27 m/s^2, the speed the car reaches on the road
options.rationale: Quotes the most prominent number back with the units asked for, without dividing.

options.text: ~240 m/s^2, from 27 m/s multiplied by the 9 s
options.rationale: Multiplies where the definition of acceleration calls for a division.

options.text: ~9 m/s^2, the same as free fall near the Earth
options.rationale: Reaches for the familiar value of g instead of using the data given.

mcqs.stem: A car of mass about 1000 kg accelerates at about 3 m/s^2. Estimate the resultant force acting on it.

options.text: ~330 N, from 1000 kg divided by 3 m/s^2
options.rationale: Divides instead of multiplying, a rearrangement error in F = m a.

options.text: ~3000 N, from 1000 kg multiplied by 3 m/s^2
options.rationale: resultant force = mass x acceleration, so the estimate is about 1000 x 3 = 3000 N, a force of a few thousand newtons.

options.text: ~10 000 N, which is the weight of the car itself
options.rationale: Estimates the weight rather than the resultant force producing the acceleration.

options.text: ~3 N, as the acceleration is about 3 m/s^2
options.rationale: Quotes the acceleration figure with the unit of force attached.

mcqs.stem: A student writes 'resultant force ~ 3000 N' at the end of an estimate. What does the symbol ~ tell the reader?

options.text: The force is smaller than 3000 N at every moment.
options.rationale: Confuses the symbol with an inequality sign from mathematics.

options.text: The force is at most 3000 N, never any higher.
options.rationale: A student reads ~ as 'no greater than', expressing m16's belief that the force is smaller than (at most) 3000 N.

options.text: The 3000 N is an approximate value, not an exact one.
options.rationale: The symbol indicates an approximate value or approximate answer, which is what an estimate from rounded data produces.

options.text: The force changes in size as the car speeds up on the road.
options.rationale: Interprets the symbol as describing the behaviour of the force rather than the precision of the figure.

mcqs.stem: In required practical activity 7, a trolley is pulled along a bench by masses hanging on a string over a pulley. When investigating how the force affects the acceleration, what must be kept constant?

options.text: The load left on the trolley.
options.rationale: A student following m17 adds masses to the hanger while leaving the trolley loaded, so they name the trolley load as the control instead of the total accelerated mass.

options.text: The acceleration of the loaded trolley.
options.rationale: Names the dependent variable as though it were a control variable.

options.text: The speed of the trolley at each gate.
options.rationale: Holding the speed constant would mean no acceleration at all, so nothing could be measured.

options.text: The total mass being accelerated.
options.rationale: The investigation varies the force on an object of constant mass, so masses are moved from the trolley to the hanger and the total accelerating mass is unchanged.

mcqs.stem: In the second part of required practical activity 7 the pulling force is kept constant and extra masses are placed on the trolley. What happens to the measured acceleration?

options.text: It stays the same, as the pulling force has not changed.
options.rationale: Fixes on the constant force and assumes the acceleration must be constant too.

options.text: It falls, because acceleration is inversely proportional to mass.
options.rationale: With a constant resultant force, a = F / m, so adding mass lowers the acceleration and a graph of acceleration against mass curves downwards.

options.text: It rises, since a heavier trolley carries more force with it.
options.rationale: Expects mass and acceleration to rise together, applying direct proportionality.

options.text: It falls to a quarter each time the mass is doubled.
options.rationale: Uses an inverse square relationship where the law gives a simple inverse one.

mcqs.stem: A swimmer pushes backwards on the water with a force of 200 N. What force does the water exert on the swimmer?

options.text: Less than 200 N, because water is pushed aside so easily.
options.rationale: Expects the sturdier object to exert the larger force in an interaction.

options.text: 400 N forwards, twice as large as the swimmer's push.
options.rationale: Doubles the force to account for two objects being involved in the interaction.

options.text: 200 N forwards, equal in size and opposite to her push.
options.rationale: Whenever two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are equal and opposite, so the water pushes forwards on the swimmer with 200 N.

options.text: 200 N backwards, in the same direction as her push.
options.rationale: Gets the size right but not the direction, so the pair is no longer opposite.

mcqs.stem: A book rests in equilibrium on a table. Which two forces form a Newton's Third Law pair?

options.text: The weight of the book and the upward push of the table on the book.
options.rationale: These are equal and opposite here, so students give them the third law label; both act on the book, so they are balanced forces.

options.text: The weight of the book and the friction between it and the table.
options.rationale: Pairs two forces at right angles to each other, neither of which forms a pair with the other.

options.text: The table's push up and the floor's push up on the table.
options.rationale: Both of these act on the table and point the same way, so they cannot be a pair.

options.text: The book's push down on the table and the table's push up on it.
options.rationale: A third law pair is the two forces two interacting objects exert on each other: here the book on the table and the table on the book, equal and opposite.

mcqs.stem: A horse pulls a cart forwards. The cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. Why does the cart still accelerate?

options.text: The two forces act on different objects.
options.rationale: A third law pair never cancels, because only forces acting on the same object can be added; the cart accelerates because of the forces acting on the cart alone.

options.text: Because the horse is far stronger than the cart is.
options.rationale: Denies that the two forces are equal, which the third law requires them to be.

options.text: It does not, so the loaded cart can never move.
options.rationale: Adds the pair together as though both forces acted on the cart.

options.text: The horse's pull comes a moment before the cart's.
options.rationale: Imagines the pair acting one after the other so that one gets a head start.
